Newborn Care

Blood clots and bleeding after birth: when to get help

Updated: October 6, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

After a baby is born, the uterus has healing to do, including at the place where the placenta was attached. Blood, mucus and tissue leave through the vagina as a discharge called lochia. Blood that collects before coming out can form a jelly-like clot. Some bleeding is expected after vaginal birth and after a cesarean, but the amount, the pattern over time and how you feel matter more than a clot’s appearance alone.

Know when to get help immediately

Seek medical care immediately for bleeding that soaks one or more pads in an hour, a clot bigger than an egg or the passage of tissue. These warnings apply on the first day too. Do not wait until 24 hours have passed, or wait for a second large clot. Smaller clots can also need assessment, especially if bleeding is increasing or you feel unwell.

Call emergency services for severe or continuing heavy bleeding, collapse, chest pain or difficulty breathing. A fever of 38°C/100.4°F or above, bad-smelling discharge, severe abdominal pain, persistent dizziness or a severe headache also requires urgent assessment. Tell the service when you gave birth. If you are still in hospital, alert staff immediately.

Why bleeding and clots occur

The uterus contracts after birth, helping close the vessels that supplied the placenta. Its lining then renews itself. Tears or cuts in the birth canal can add to blood loss after a vaginal birth. The discharge is therefore more than ordinary menstrual blood, and its appearance can change as recovery progresses.

A clot may contain mucus or tissue as well as blood, but you cannot reliably identify what it contains by looking at it. Nor can you determine at home whether every part of the placenta has passed. Describe or show a concerning clot to your maternity team when practical; never delay urgent care to collect, measure or photograph it.

The first 24 hours

Bleeding is usually at its greatest just after birth and may look red or reddish brown. Maternity staff assess the loss, how firmly the uterus is contracting and your general condition. Let them know about a sudden gush, a large clot or feeling faint, even if you have been told to expect a heavier flow than a period.

A description such as tomato-sized or golf-ball-sized is not reassurance that a clot is normal. Soaking a pad each hour should not be treated as an expected part of day-one recovery. Heavy loss can need treatment promptly, and the first day is not an exception.

Days two to six

Across the next few days, the overall amount should decrease. The colour often becomes darker brown or pinkish red. A small clot can sometimes pass, but new, repeated or enlarging clots should be discussed with the maternity team. A change to brown does not prove there is no ongoing bleeding.

Watch the trend rather than comparing your pad with a precise stain measurement. Different pads absorb different amounts. If bleeding becomes heavier instead of settling, or pain, fever or an unpleasant smell develops, seek advice promptly. Do not wait for the next scheduled postnatal visit.

Days seven to fourteen

During days seven to ten, lochia is often lighter in colour and quantity. During days eleven to fourteen it may be lighter again, with some pads barely marked. These stages overlap: everyone does not switch colour on the same date.

Activity can briefly make the loss more noticeable. Reduce exertion and follow your recovery advice, but do not explain away a significant increase as merely doing too much. Continuing moderate-to-heavy loss, repeated clots or a return to heavy red bleeding needs assessment. The calendar alone cannot establish that recovery is going well.

Weeks three to six and the return of periods

By the third and fourth weeks, discharge is often much smaller in amount and may look creamy, pale or lightly blood-stained. In weeks five and six, some people have stopped bleeding, while others still notice occasional pink, brown or yellowish staining. Six weeks is an approximate recovery landmark, not a guaranteed finishing date.

Menstrual periods return at different times. Feeding patterns can affect the timing, and a period can restart within the early postpartum weeks. However, fresh bleeding should not automatically be labelled a period if it is heavy, painful or accompanied by illness. Ask for a review when the pattern is not clearly improving or you are uncertain.

Why the amount may vary during the day

After lying down overnight, blood that has collected can come out when you stand. During a breastfeed, hormones make the uterus contract; you may notice cramps and a temporary change in the flow. A busier day can also make lochia more noticeable.

These explanations help describe small variations, but none cancels the warning signs. Tell the team whether a change occurred after feeding, getting up or exercise, and whether it settled. You do not need to stop breastfeeding merely because lochia is present; significant bleeding calls for assessment of you and support with feeding as needed.

Other changes that deserve a call

A wound or stitches that appear to open, increasing tenderness, worsening pelvic pain or a new offensive smell should be reported. Red blood after day three is not, by itself, a diagnosis of a complication; what matters is whether the loss is heavy, becoming greater or occurring with other symptoms.

Keep your maternity contact details accessible after discharge. Explain the number of pads used, whether they were soaked, the size and frequency of any clots and how you feel. Mention medicines, including blood thinners, and any complication during birth. If you cannot reach your usual team and symptoms are urgent, use the local urgent or emergency service.

Vaginal clots and clots in blood vessels are different

A clot passed through the vagina is not the same as a deep vein thrombosis, or DVT. A DVT forms within a deep vein, often in a leg or the pelvis. Pregnancy and recent birth increase this risk, although these clots remain uncommon. A clot can travel to the lungs and cause a pulmonary embolism.

New swelling, warmth or pain affecting one leg needs urgent medical attention. Sudden breathlessness, chest pressure, coughing blood or collapse is an emergency. Sudden one-sided weakness, numbness, loss of balance or a severe new headache also needs emergency assessment for a possible neurological event. These symptoms are not explained by normal lochia; do not wait for vaginal bleeding to occur.

How abnormal bleeding is assessed

The team first considers how much blood you may be losing and whether you are stable. They may check your pulse and blood pressure, examine the abdomen and birth injuries, take blood samples or use an ultrasound when indicated. Ultrasound can help investigate remaining placental tissue, but it is not automatically needed for every small clot.

Possible causes include a uterus that is not contracting effectively, tissue left in the uterus, an injury or infection. Heavy bleeding can happen immediately or develop after discharge. In RCOG terminology, secondary postpartum hemorrhage can occur from 24 hours to 12 weeks after birth, so leaving the hospital or passing the six-week mark does not make abnormal bleeding safe.

Treatment depends on the cause and severity

If the uterus is not contracting adequately, clinicians may use medicines and other measures to help it contract and control the bleeding. An injury may require repair; infection may need antibiotics. Remaining placental tissue sometimes needs removal under anesthesia. The term dilation and curettage, or D&C, refers to one possible procedure, not the inevitable treatment for any clot.

Severe loss may require intravenous fluids, blood transfusion or further procedures to stop bleeding. The team should explain what is happening and why treatment is recommended. Do not try to remove tissue, perform uterine massage or take medicines to stop the bleeding on your own. Pads manage the discharge; they do not treat a hemorrhage.

Everyday care while healing

Use maternity or period pads and change them regularly. Wash your hands before and after changing a pad or using the toilet, and avoid unnecessary handling of stitches or dressings. Wait until healing has been assessed before returning to internal period products; NHS advice is to avoid tampons until after the six-week postnatal check.

You do not need to purchase a particular cooling pad to recover. Ask the maternity team about comfortable perineal care and suitable pain relief if needed. Drink normally, eat a varied diet and ask about constipation treatment if passing stool is difficult. A stool softener or laxative may improve bowel comfort, but does not prevent uterine clots or treat excessive bleeding.

Balance rest, movement and prescribed clot prevention

Arrange help with lifting and household work so you can rest, then return to movement gradually according to your birth and recovery plan. Complete bed rest is not a routine way to prevent clots. Gentle mobility and avoiding dehydration support recovery, while persistent or increasing bleeding should prompt a call rather than repeated attempts to manage it through rest alone.

Compression stockings and blood-thinning injections are recommended for some people after an individual risk assessment. Use the prescribed type and duration; do not start or stop them independently because you see lochia. Raising your legs may help comfort but does not replace assessment of one-sided swelling or prescribed prevention. Measures for vein clots and treatment of uterine bleeding serve different purposes.

Follow up after significant blood loss

If you needed treatment for a hemorrhage, ask about your blood count, iron replacement, follow-up and what symptoms should trigger another call. Recovery can take time, and practical help with meals, sleep and baby care may be important. Feeling persistently faint or increasingly weak should be assessed rather than attributed automatically to newborn tiredness.

It can also help to talk through a frightening birth or emergency treatment with the team. Ask what caused the bleeding, what was done and whether it affects planning for a future pregnancy. A clear discharge plan should tell you whom to contact and how to obtain support while you recover.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

CDC warning signs require immediate assessment for excessive postpartum blood loss and associated systemic symptoms.

NHS guidance describes gradual changes in lochia and practical care; timelines are approximate.

RCOG distinguishes uterine hemorrhage from venous thrombosis and describes cause-dependent treatment.

How BeMama can help

The source’s full recovery timeline, warning signs, causes, treatments and practical advice are retained with explicit corrections to unsafe reassurance and clot-prevention claims.

When to seek help

Educational information; not a way to diagnose bleeding at home. Clinical obstetric review remains pending before publication.

Evidence notes updated: October 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Lochia should generally diminish, but its colour and duration vary.
  • Large clots, heavy bleeding or feeling unwell need assessment even on the first day.
  • A week-by-week guide cannot establish whether bleeding is safe.
  • Clots inside veins are different from clots passed vaginally and have separate warning signs.
  • Pads, hydration and rest support recovery; they do not treat a postpartum hemorrhage.

Frequently asked questions

Can I pass a large clot normally in the first 24 hours?

Do not assume it is harmless. Tell the maternity team immediately about a large clot or heavy bleeding, including on the day of birth.

What if a clot is smaller than an egg?

Size is only one warning sign. Repeated clots, increasing bleeding, pain or feeling unwell can require assessment even when each clot is smaller.

Does brown blood mean bleeding has definitely stopped?

No. Brown often reflects older blood, but colour alone does not measure the amount being lost or rule out a complication.

Should all bleeding stop by six weeks?

No exact stopping date applies to everyone. A light, improving discharge can last longer, but worsening or heavy bleeding should be reviewed rather than waiting for a deadline.

Why do I notice more blood after getting out of bed?

Collected blood may come out on standing. A small temporary change can occur, but a large gush, repeated clots or symptoms of illness should not be dismissed for that reason.

Do I bleed vaginally after a cesarean?

Yes. The inside of the uterus still heals after the placenta is delivered, even when the baby was born through an abdominal incision.

Does a vaginal clot mean I have a clot in my leg?

No. They are different processes. One-sided leg swelling or pain needs assessment independently of whether you have vaginal bleeding.

Will every clot require a D&C?

No. Assessment determines whether treatment is needed and what kind. A procedure may be appropriate for retained tissue, but cannot be decided from clot appearance alone.

Can drinking water or using compression stockings stop lochia?

No. Normal hydration and prescribed stockings may support recovery or reduce vein-clot risk. They are not treatments for abnormal uterine bleeding.

What should I say when I call for help?

Give the date and type of birth, explain the bleeding and clots, list other symptoms and mention relevant medicines. Do not delay an emergency call while gathering every detail.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
